07-M1.verdict_why: Two lines converge but neither tests this rule. Automatic extraction of concepts and their relations from instructional text is repeatedly demonstrated (07-M1-c3, 07-M1-c2), and structured node-link maps are associated with better retention and science achievement (07-M1-c27, 07-M1-c30 — correlational, and mostly learner-constructed or viewed maps, not model-generated course outlines). Against, 07-M1-c18 reports that automatic concept-map mining from material produces generic maps that fit teacher intent poorly. Guidance/structure helps inquiry learning (07-M1-c28) but does not address window-by-window planning from a user's file. No candidate compares learning from one's own material versus provided material, and none tests a 350-character or 30-skill cap.
07-M1.code_vs_evidence: The general principle — machine-extracted concepts and ordered structure from text can support study — is backed, but only at the level of feasibility and of human-built maps. The specific rules are design choices with no direct evidence: one skill per 350 characters and a 30-skill cap are unstudied chunking parameters, and 07-M1-c18 warns that automatic structuring of a document can yield generic, context-poor units. Ordering 'in the material's own order' is not tested against prerequisite-inferred ordering, which 07-M1-c2 shows is learnable but error-prone. The syllabus-only-topic rule (teaching named topics from general knowledge, labelled as such) has no support in these abstracts and carries an unaddressed accuracy risk. The headline claim that learning from one's own uploaded material beats provided material is a gap: no candidate study addresses it.

07-M2.verdict_why: Evidence converges that prerequisite relations exist and can be inferred automatically (Pan 2017; Manrique 2019; Bai 2025 survey), and that hierarchies can be necessary for some skills (White 1973, reviewing Gagné's seven-child study). But White's companion paper limits the 'essential prerequisite' claim to intellectual skills, treating other knowledge as merely helpful precursors, which conflicts with gating every skill on mastery; and none of the abstracts test whether a mastery-locked path raises learning outcomes, nor how accurate automatic prerequisite inference is in a real curriculum.
07-M2.code_vs_evidence: Partly aligned. Ordering prerequisites first matches the hierarchy and prerequisite-learning literature, and automatic prerequisite inference is plausible but the app's skill list is authored, not validated as Pan/Manrique validate theirs. Two gaps: (1) strict mastery gating is a design choice — the sources show prerequisites matter most for procedural/intellectual skills and only as helpful precursors elsewhere, so a hard lock on factual skills is stronger than the evidence; (2) no cited study measures learning gains from the gating rule itself, and the fallback of otherwise keeping the material's order is untested. A softer option — warn or suggest rather than lock, and let mastery thresholds be revisited — would fit the evidence better.

07-M3.verdict_why: The efficiency premise is well supported: adaptive testing is repeatedly described as reaching comparable precision with fewer items (c6, c9), and Bayesian learner modeling has empirical backing (c25) plus a large knowledge-space evaluation (c10). But the app's exact rule -- skip every skill the belief marks known, then one quick check, a miss earning a second question -- has no direct study here. And the testing-effect review (c28) cuts the other way: skipped skills lose retrieval practice, so the review step is doing real work rather than being cosmetic.
07-M3.code_vs_evidence: Partly matches. Information-maximizing item selection over a probabilistic belief state matches CAT and Bayesian learner-modeling evidence, and prerequisite propagation is consistent with knowledge-space assessment work. Gaps: (1) the hard skip rule is a design choice, not a validated one, and c28 suggests skipped-but-known skills still benefit from being tested rather than only reviewed; (2) the specific priors -- 10% slip, guessing plus 15 points of luck, a shared right-answer rate -- are unvalidated in the supplied abstracts, and c9 notes bias correction matters early in a test when few items have been answered; (3) the 'one quick check, miss earns a second' stopping rule has no evidence attached, so its false-negative cost for a truly known skill is unmeasured.

07-M4.verdict_why: The general principle the mechanism relies on — matching the amount of guidance to the learner's prior knowledge — has converging support, including a recent meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect (Tetzlaff 2025, 60 experiments) plus Kalyuga's review and Leppink's prior-knowledge interaction. The 'harder is better' half is weaker: desirable-difficulty reviews say difficulties may help long-term retention, but studies such as Dobson 2011 found no benefit from specific difficulty manipulations, and Lazonder's guidance meta-analysis shows guidance is broadly facilitative without confirmed expertise moderation. No study tests the exact rules (one perfect check moves up one tier, failed check moves down, reviews at tier 2+, Elo pace reducing question count), so the precise mechanics remain design choices rather than validated procedure.
07-M4.code_vs_evidence: Partly matches. Adaptive support by prior knowledge is consistent with the ATI/expertise-reversal meta-analysis, so starting half-known skills at tier 2 and reducing scaffolding for advanced learners is evidence-aligned. Gaps: (1) a single perfect check as the trigger for moving up a tier is untested and noisy — evidence ties guidance level to prior knowledge, not to one-item performance; (2) the tier ladder assumes combining/transfer items are always the better goal, but transfer tasks are not uniformly superior for retention (Dobson 2011 found no interleaving/expanding-retrieval benefit); (3) the 'reviews ask tier 2 or above' rule predicts benefit from harder review, which desirable-difficulty reviews frame as 'may' help long-term retention, not as established; (4) the Elo-style pace reducing the number of practice questions for fast learners is not addressed by any of these sources — no candidate study examines Elo ratings for learners or items, so that element is unsupported here; (5) Lazonder's finding that guidance is generally facilitative cautions against pulling support too aggressively on a short performance signal.

07-M5.verdict_why: The general principle has converging meta-analytic support (Kulik 1990: 108 controlled evaluations, positive examination effects, strongest for weaker students) and a small quasi-experiment in physics, but Slavin's best-evidence synthesis (1990) found essentially no effect on standardized achievement and only a small effect on experimenter-made tests, so the size and durability of the benefit is contested rather than settled. No source studies the specific rule of 75% on about five items with feedback withheld until the end, so that threshold and test length are a design choice, not an evidence-based finding; Pelanek (2018) shows thresholds and data sources are consequential and need justification.
07-M5.code_vs_evidence: Direction of the general principle matches the evidence, with two gaps. (1) Gating on prerequisites and remediation loops fits Bloom's corrective-feedback logic described by Guskey (2007), but the app's check gives no feedback until the end and is only about five questions: with five items, 75% means four of five correct, one item swings the decision by 20 points, and Pelanek's work indicates that such threshold decisions depend heavily on the amount and kind of evidence, so a single five-item check may misclassify learners. The corrective-feedback part of mastery learning is delayed rather than built into the check. (2) Cost and completion: Kulik reports mastery programmes may increase student time on instructional tasks and that self-paced mastery programmes often reduce completion rates in college classes; Post (2023) notes attainment of a mastery level carries a measurable per-student cost. Locking the next skill until a 75% check is passed, without evidence on the threshold or item count, is a plausible design choice rather than a finding, and the app should expect longer time on task and possible drop-off. Groen (2015) adds a caution that test-oriented mastery can shift learners toward passing checks rather than deeper understanding.

07-M6.verdict_why: Elaborated feedback is supported by two meta-analyses, and distractor-based diagnosis has review support. Refutation-text evidence is mixed: one undergraduate study found fewer misconceptions, but a grade 9 study found a plain didactic text worked as well. A biology-education essay also cautions against framing misconceptions as things to eradicate. No source tests the exact rule of keeping a misconception and showing it again, or of putting missed questions first in the next check.
07-M6.code_vs_evidence: The app's elaboration after a miss and its use of wrong choices as diagnostic signals match the feedback and distractor literature. The refutation component is plausible but not reliably superior to clear explanation, and the 'misconception' framing should avoid implying deletion of naive ideas. The missed-questions-first rule and cross-lesson persistence of the misconception label are not directly tested by these sources; feedback should be specific, nonevaluative, and timed appropriately.

07-M7.verdict_why: Two meta-analyses and a systematic review of classroom experiments converge on retrieval practice beating restudy (c1, c2, c18), and a narrative review of applied classroom work reaches the same general conclusion (c22). The conflicts are narrower than they look: c19 found no benefit in one primary-school vocabulary programme, and c13 shows feedback can reverse the testing advantage when practice retrieval success is low. So the core retrieval-practice principle is well supported; the feedback-after-every-question element is the weaker, less settled part of the mechanism, and the abstracts do not establish an optimal feedback schedule.
07-M7.code_vs_evidence: The app's core rule (questions answered from memory instead of re-reading, then explanation and quote shown) matches the general testing-effect evidence. Gaps: (1) the abstracts do not test giving the explanation and quote immediately after every single item; c13 and c22 indicate feedback effects depend on retrieval success and schedule, so 'always show it right away' is a design choice, not a verified rule; (2) nothing here tests the app's exact format, spacing, or the explanation+quote combination; (3) c19 shows retrieval practice can fail in authentic school lessons, so the app should not promise benefits in every subject or age group.

07-M8.verdict_why: There is converging, high-quality evidence for the general principle in mathematics: a preregistered cluster RCT in 7th-grade classes (d = 0.83), an earlier 7th-grade experiment, a meta-analysis showing the benefit depends on similarity/complexity of what is mixed, a systematic review finding benefits greatest for subtle differences and on delayed tests, and a physics study with surprise tests. One study in a different domain (critical reasoning) found no interleaving benefit, so the support is domain-dependent rather than universal. No source tests this app's specific rule (exactly one due earlier-skill item per new-skill check, miss advances the review), so the implementation details are design choices extrapolated from the general finding.
07-M8.code_vs_evidence: Direction matches: mixing earlier material into practice and testing without cueing which strategy is needed is what the math RCTs and meta-analyses tested. Gaps: (1) The evidence interleaves whole assignments so no two consecutive problems use the same strategy; the app inserts a single earlier-skill item into a new-skill check, a much lighter dose whose size is untested. (2) Selecting the item 'closest to falling due' is spaced-repetition scheduling logic, not something these studies varied. (3) Advancing a review after a miss is plausible corrective feedback but is not what the interleaving studies measured. (4) The moderators warn that mixing only helps when the mixed material is similar enough to invite discrimination and is not well suited to expository or vocabulary material, so pair items that are genuinely confusable rather than arbitrary. (5) Learners misjudge interleaving as harder and less effective (physics study), so expectations may need framing. (6) Order may matter in math: one fraction study suggests blocking in a prerequisite-first order can sometimes beat interleaving, so avoid interleaving material whose prerequisites are not yet mastered.

07-M10.verdict_why: Several studies show LLM-generated MCQs can reach expert-rated quality close to human items, especially with structured prompts grounded in source material, but quality varies by model and item-writing flaws persist, and the abstracts show item ratings rather than learning outcomes. No candidate tested the specific rules here: the untrusted-data instruction against prompt injection, the 6 to 9 item count, or position bias of correct answers in LLM-generated items. The shuffling rule rests on broader distractor-ordering and exam-scrambling research, not on studies of model answer-position bias.
07-M10.code_vs_evidence: Partly matches. Generating questions only from the skill's passages with a structured instruction is consistent with prompt-pattern and source-grounded generation findings, and shuffling options is a defensible precaution against any systematic ordering, but the evidence for option-order effects comes from human-written items and surveys, not LLM outputs. The prompt-injection defense ('treat material as untrusted data') is an engineering safeguard with no cited empirical support here, and no source shows that model-generated lessons improve learning. Gaps: no evidence on learner outcomes from LLM-written lessons, no validation of item count or difficulty calibration, and no study of answer-position bias specific to generated MCQs; expert or automated item review before use would be a reasonable addition.

07-M11.verdict_why: Surveys and reviews converge that LLM generation hallucinates and that grounding in retrieved source text plus attribution is a recognized mitigation direction (c1, c2, c19, c3), and c21 shows fabricated references are common enough that a literal find-in-source check has a real job. But no abstract here tests this exact rule: a minimum of 20 letters-and-digits, dropping rather than repairing the question, and tying a merely-named topic to the line that names it. c4 also shows that citation presence is not the same as citation sufficiency, so the rule's guarantee is narrower than 'the question is supported by the source'.
07-M11.code_vs_evidence: The app's check is a literal substring test on the question's own passage, which matches the general principle of grounding and attribution and echoes the fabrication problem in c21, but the evidence does not validate the threshold: a 20-character string such as a short phrase or a bare named term passes without supporting the question's claim, and c4 indicates citation support is incomplete even in systems built for it. Dropping the question with no model call is a conservative design choice not studied here; nothing in these abstracts shows that a verified quote in the passage makes the question answerable from that quote, nor that tying a named-only topic to its naming line produces a useful question rather than a trivially grounded one.

07-M12.verdict_why: The general principle is well supported: strong judges approach human agreement on open-ended evaluation (c1), diverse-family panels beat a single judge with less intra-model bias (c2), and verification passes reduce hallucination on factuality tasks (c3). But the evidence conflicts on the app's specific proof setup: jury gains over single judges were small and context-dependent in a non-English health setting (c7), judges track humans mainly on objective criteria (c12), and reliability is described as a design and standardization challenge rather than a given (c10). The exact rules - fail-closed only on 'supported: true', regenerate once below 3 items, planted-error catch-rate audits - are not directly studied by any candidate, so the precise thresholds are a design choice.
07-M12.code_vs_evidence: Partly matches. Checking grounded support against the passage is the kind of objective, factuality-style criterion where judges align best with humans (c12), and using models from other families for the audit matches the disjoint-family panel finding (c2). Gaps: the production gate is a single second model, whereas c2 favors panels over one judge, and a same-family checker is exposed to the self-enhancement and position/verbosity biases documented in c1; c3's verification gains come from the same model deliberating, mostly on factuality benchmarks, not from an independent passage-grounded checker. The audit measures catch rate on planted wrong answers, which is cleaner than real errors, and c7 warns that jury gains can be marginal and degrade outside English, so per-item 'supported: true' with a 3-item floor should be treated as an untested design choice rather than an evidence-backed threshold.

07-M13.verdict_why: No source tests this exact rule set (delete-with-course, text-only retention, no outside model for children without consent, answer keys withheld). Survey and conceptual work converge on consent, transparency and perceived control mattering to students (c10, c9, c1), and child-specific guidance exists but lags general AI ethics (c18, c23). Against the design's technological framing, c3 argues control-based technical fixes rest on assumptions and need institutional governance; c23 says balancing privacy and data use is not easily supported by current regulation. So principle-level support with a real caveat, not converging trials.
07-M13.code_vs_evidence: Matches the evidence in direction: minimisation, single-account scoping, user-initiated deletion, consent-gated outside AI for minors and withholding answer keys all align with the control/consent principles students report valuing (c9, c10) and with child-specific rights concerns (c23). Gaps: (1) the evidence is about perceptions and principles, not measured outcomes of these specific rules, so no claim of proven benefit is warranted; (2) deletion of course and progress at once may be defensible under minimisation but no source here tested its effect on learners, and c3 warns that technical controls presuppose institutional governance, consent records and accountability outside the app; (3) 'children without consent get no outside model' relies on verifiable consent and age assurance, which none of the abstracts show is solved; (4) withholding answer keys is an assessment-integrity measure, not addressed by any cited source, so it is a design choice, not an evidence-backed one.
